verifyNote: Written from standard research methods and evidence-based practice teaching. Always check against Dr Collins's slides and the library workshop materials — terminology and preferred tests can differ.

topics.title: Experimental and research design
topics.summary: From Prof Meese's week 9 lecture and the week 4 library session: designing an experiment means framing testable hypotheses, choosing and controlling variables, avoiding floor and ceiling effects and confounds, picking a participant design and controlling order effects. Know the main study designs too.
keyPoints: Turn a vague idea into testable hypotheses: H1 (e.g. alcohol degrades visuo-motor performance) and H0 (it doesn't). One-tailed predicts a direction; two-tailed predicts any change.
We try to falsify H0: a hypothesis can be disproved but never proven, and there's only one null to compare data against.

Variables: independent (manipulated; its levels are conditions, often with a control), dependent (measured), confounding (changes with the IV, which wastes the experiment) and extraneous (held constant).
Not every experiment needs a control condition, e.g. measuring the contrast sensitivity function across spatial frequencies.
Floor effect: the task is too hard to show a drop. Ceiling effect: too easy to show a change. Pilot studies set levels and doses.
Placebos remove the confound of knowing your condition (single-blind); in double-blind studies the experimenter doesn't know either.
Within-subjects designs remove differences between people; between-subjects is needed for sex or age comparisons or very long experiments.
Order effects (fatigue, learning): counterbalance (half each order) or use randomised blocks when there are many levels.

Study designs from the library session: systematic reviews and meta-analyses, RCTs, cohort, case-control, cross-sectional, case reports and series, longitudinal studies, narrative reviews, guidelines, expert opinion.
examTraps: Thinking an experiment with an identified confound can still be interpreted: it can't.
Using a between-subjects design when within-subjects is possible.
Leaving order effects uncontrolled.

diagram.description: Pyramid with layers from bottom to top: expert opinion; case reports/series; cross-sectional; case-control; cohort; randomised controlled trials; systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: observational designs and bias
goDeeper.body: RCTs randomise allocation to balance known and unknown confounders. Cohort studies follow people with and without an exposure; case-control studies start from the outcome and look back (good for rare conditions); cross-sectional studies give a snapshot of prevalence. Common biases: selection, measurement or observer, recall and attrition.

flashcards.back: To balance known and unknown confounders between groups.

flashcards.front: Best design for a rare disease's risk factors
flashcards.back: Case-control study.
Prevalence and associations at one time point (not cause).
A third factor linked to both the exposure and the outcome.
Single: participants don't know their condition (e.g. a placebo). Double: the experimenter doesn't know either.

flashcards.front: When must you use a between-subjects design?
flashcards.back: Comparing sexes or age groups, or when there are too many conditions for one person to do.
Half the participants do condition A first and half do B first, so order effects cancel out.

mcq.q: Researchers compare 200 people with keratoconus and 200 without, asking about past eye rubbing. What design is this?

options.feedback: Yes — start with the outcome, look back at exposure.
A cohort starts from exposure and follows forward.

mcq.explanation: Case-control studies start with people who have the condition and compare past exposures with controls.

mcq.q: Which method assesses agreement between two tonometers?

options.feedback: Right — it plots differences against means.
It can show bias but not limits of agreement.

mcq.explanation: Bland–Altman shows mean bias and 95% limits of agreement between two measurement methods.

mcq.q: The experimental variable is

options.text: another name for the independent variable
the variable measured by the experimenter
a variable that confounds the results

mcq.q: A dependent variable rises with the independent variable, but a confounding variable is then found. Which is true?

options.text: There could really be a negative relationship between the DV and the IV
options.feedback: Yes: the confound could be masking an opposite effect. You can't separate them.

options.text: The result can't be statistically significant
options.feedback: It can be significant; it just can't be interpreted.

options.text: The result is sound because the confound has been identified
The confound must have influenced the results
options.feedback: It might have; you can't tell.

mcq.q: A floor effect is when

options.text: control results are so low that the IV couldn't produce meaningfully lower values
options.feedback: Yes: the task is too hard to show a drop.

options.text: the experimental condition is as easy as the control
a confounding variable must have influenced the results

mcq.q: Your hypothesis is that caffeine changes reaction time, without saying in which direction. This is

options.feedback: Yes: any change counts, so both tails are tested.
One-tailed predicts a direction, e.g. 'caffeine speeds reactions'.
The null is 'caffeine doesn't change reaction time'.
That's something held constant, not a prediction.

mcq.q: Why do experimenters set out to falsify the null hypothesis rather than prove the experimental one?

options.text: A hypothesis can be disproved but never proven, and there's only one null to test against
options.feedback: Yes: the moorhen example, and the single comparison with a mean difference of zero.
It may well be false; that's what we test.

options.text: Statistics software can only test nulls
options.feedback: It's a logical point, not a software limit.

mcq.q: In the darts experiment, participants know when they've had alcohol because only then are they handed a cup. What's the best fix?

options.text: Give a placebo drink that looks, tastes and smells the same
options.feedback: Yes: that removes the confound of knowing the condition (single-blind).
More people don't remove a confound.

options.text: Test everyone at the same time of day
options.feedback: That controls an extraneous variable, not this confound.

mcq.q: Every participant in your study does the alcohol condition first and the control second. What problem does this create?

options.text: Order effects (fatigue or learning) are confounded with condition
options.feedback: Yes: counterbalance so half do each order.

mcq.q: You need to measure sensitivity at 12 spatial frequencies, four times each, in the same people. How should you order the conditions?

options.text: Randomised blocks: each block tests every frequency once in a new random order
options.feedback: Yes: full counterbalancing is impractical with so many levels.

options.text: Always test from low to high frequency
options.feedback: That builds in an order effect.

options.text: Toss a coin for each participant
options.feedback: Chance can still leave an imbalance; with 12 levels you need blocks.

options.text: Test each frequency four times in a row
options.feedback: Fatigue and learning would differ between frequencies.

topics.askClaude: Describe 5 eye research studies in one sentence each and ask me to name the design and one possible bias for each.

topics.title: Descriptive and inferential statistics
topics.summary: From Prof Meese's week 10 lecture and handout: describe data with means, SDs and SEs, use inferential tests (t-test, ANOVA) to get p, interpret significance carefully, decide one- or two-tailed in advance, and be wary of intuition about risk.
keyPoints: Two data sets can share a mean but differ in spread: the standard deviation describes spread. SE = SD ÷ √n describes how precisely the mean is known; plotted means usually show ±1 SE.
p is the probability of results at least this extreme if H0 were true (0 ≤ p ≤ 1). p ≤ 0.05 is significant; p ≤ 0.01 highly significant.
If significant, reject H0 and say you 'have evidence to support' H1: chance can never be ruled out.
Statistical significance isn't scientific or clinical importance.
A two-tailed test splits the 5% between both tails; one-tailed puts it in one. Decide before collecting data; registered reports stop people switching afterwards.
Use a t-test for two conditions and ANOVA (F ratio, same p interpretation) for more levels or factors, including interactions. Non-parametric tests exist for data that break parametric assumptions.
People judge big and small probabilities badly: '100 times the risk' needs the baseline, and every lottery combination (even 1–6) is equally unlikely.
examTraps: Thinking p < 0.05 proves H1.
Thinking SE is bigger than SD.
Calling t a descriptive statistic.

diagram.description: Bell-shaped normal distribution with the mean at the centre and shaded bands at ±1 SD (68%), ±2 SD (95%) and ±3 SD (99.7%).

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: more on statistics
goDeeper.body: Medians and interquartile ranges suit skewed data. In a normal distribution about 68% lies within ±1 SD and 95% within ±1.96 SD; a 95% confidence interval is about mean ± 1.96 SE. Type I error is a false positive (α), type II a false negative (β), and power = 1 − β. Non-parametric equivalents include Wilcoxon signed-rank and Mann-Whitney U; chi-squared is for categories.

flashcards.back: SE = SD ÷ √n.
False positive (rejecting a true null hypothesis).
Paired t-test.

flashcards.front: Non-parametric test for two independent groups
flashcards.back: Mann–Whitney U.
SD ÷ √n: how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean.

flashcards.front: What ANOVA reports instead of t
flashcards.back: An F ratio, with a p value interpreted the same way.
'100 times the risk' of a 1-in-100-million event is still only 1 in a million.

mcq.q: IOP is measured in the same 30 people before and after a new drop; the differences are normally distributed. Which test?
mcq.explanation: Repeated measures on the same participants with normally distributed differences → paired t-test.

mcq.q: A screening test has high sensitivity. What does that mean?

options.text: It correctly identifies most people who have the condition
It correctly clears most people without the condition
A positive result is almost always correct
options.feedback: That's positive predictive value, which depends on prevalence.

options.text: It gives the same answer when repeated

mcq.explanation: Sensitivity = true positives ÷ all with the disease.

mcq.q: Which is TRUE?

options.text: If a one-tailed test in the predicted direction isn't significant, a two-tailed test won't be either
options.feedback: Yes: the two-tailed cut-off is stricter in each tail.

options.text: A result is significant if p > 1/20
A highly significant result can't have come about by chance
options.feedback: Chance can never be ruled out completely.

options.text: The SE is usually larger than the SD
options.feedback: SE = SD ÷ √n, so it's smaller once n > 1.

options.text: Two data sets differ significantly if their means are very different
options.feedback: It depends on the spread and n too.

mcq.q: In analysis of variance (ANOVA)

options.text: main effects and interactions can be investigated across three independent variables
only two levels of each IV can be tested
there must be a control condition

mcq.q: Which is NOT a descriptive statistic?

options.feedback: Yes: t comes from an inferential test.

mcq.q: A main purpose of a registered report is to

options.text: make sure one-tailed testing isn't chosen after the fact
options.feedback: Yes: the plan is fixed before the data are collected.

mcq.q: Data set A is 9, 10, 11 and set B is 1, 10, 19. Which statement is true?

options.text: They have the same mean but B has a larger standard deviation
options.feedback: Yes: both means are 10; B is far more spread out.

options.text: They have the same mean and the same SD

mcq.q: A sample has SD 4 and n = 16. What is the standard error?
A result is statistically significant at p < 0.05. Which conclusion is best?

options.text: We have evidence to support the experimental hypothesis
options.feedback: Yes: we reject the null but haven't proven anything.
Science doesn't prove; chance can't be ruled out.
Significance isn't the same as clinical importance.

options.text: There is a 95% chance the experimental hypothesis is true

mcq.q: A newspaper says a food makes a rare disease 100 times more likely. What do you need before judging the risk?

options.feedback: Yes: 100 × one in 100 million is still only one in a million.
That doesn't tell you the size of the risk.
Relative risk without the baseline is misleading.

topics.askClaude: Give me 6 mini research questions with data descriptions and ask me which statistical test to use and why.

topics.title: Reading and critiquing a paper
topics.summary: Critical appraisal means judging whether a study's results are trustworthy and useful. Use a structured checklist (such as CASP) and work through the question, design, methods, results and how far you can apply them to your patients.
keyPoints: Papers usually follow IMRaD: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion.
Is there a clear, focused question (PICO: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome)?
Is the design appropriate for the question?
Methods: how were participants selected? Randomised? Masked? Was follow-up complete?
Results: how big is the effect and how precise (confidence intervals)? Is it clinically meaningful, not just statistically significant?
Applicability: are the participants like your patients? Are the outcomes relevant?
Check funding, conflicts of interest, peer review and the journal's credibility.
examTraps: Appraising from the abstract alone.
Equating statistical significance with clinical importance.
Ignoring dropouts and loss to follow-up.

diagram.description: A paper shaped like an hourglass: broad Introduction narrowing to the specific question, Methods and Results in the narrow middle, Discussion widening back out to implications. Side notes list appraisal questions for each part.

goDeeper.heading: Clinical vs statistical significance
goDeeper.body: A huge study can find a 'significant' IOP difference of 0.3 mmHg that makes no difference to patients. A small study may find a large, important effect that isn't statistically significant because it's underpowered. Look at the effect size and its confidence interval, and ask whether it would change what you do.

goDeeper.heading: Spotting weak evidence
goDeeper.body: Warning signs: no control group, outcomes chosen after seeing the data, large dropouts, small samples with big claims, results only reported as p-values, industry funding with no independent replication, or conclusions that go beyond the data.

flashcards.back: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion.
Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome.

flashcards.front: A widely used UK appraisal checklist
flashcards.back: CASP (Critical Appraisal Skills Programme).

flashcards.front: What shows size and precision of an effect?
flashcards.back: The effect size with its confidence interval.

mcq.q: A trial of 5,000 people reports a statistically significant 0.1 D difference in refraction between two lenses. Best interpretation?

options.text: Statistically significant but probably not clinically meaningful
options.feedback: Yes — 0.1 D is below what most patients notice.
Large samples can make tiny effects significant.

mcq.explanation: Statistical significance tells you the effect probably isn't zero, not that it matters clinically.

mcq.q: A trial reports a statistically significant improvement of 0.02 logMAR. What should you consider first?

options.text: Whether such a small change is clinically meaningful
options.feedback: Yes: statistical and clinical significance differ (0.02 logMAR is one letter).
Not relevant to the size of the effect.

mcq.q: Which feature most strengthens a randomised controlled trial?

options.text: Allocation concealed and outcome assessors masked
options.feedback: Yes: it limits selection and detection bias.

options.text: Recruiting only volunteers who prefer the new treatment
Analysing only those who completed the trial
options.feedback: That risks attrition bias; intention-to-treat is better.

mcq.q: 30% of participants in one arm of a trial drop out, compared with 5% in the other. What's the main concern?

options.feedback: Yes: unequal loss can skew the comparison.
That affects case-control studies asking about the past.
That's about which studies get published.

mcq.q: A case-control study asks people with and without cataract how much time they spent in the sun as children. What bias is most likely?

options.feedback: Yes: people with a disease may remember exposures differently.
That's about treatment delivery in trials.

mcq.q: Why does randomisation help in a trial?

options.text: It balances known and unknown confounders between groups
It makes the result statistically significant
It removes the need for a control group
It means participants can't drop out

mcq.q: A study finds people who carry lighters get more lung cancer. What's the most likely explanation?

options.feedback: Yes: smoking is linked to both lighter-carrying and lung cancer.
A consistent link like this is confounding.

mcq.q: Which result gives the most precise estimate of an effect?

options.feedback: Yes: narrow intervals mean precise estimates.
p doesn't tell you precision directly.
Size and precision are different things.

mcq.q: What does a conflict of interest statement tell you?

options.text: Whether authors have interests (e.g. funding) that could bias the work
options.feedback: Yes: worth weighing when you read the results.

options.text: That the study was peer reviewed

mcq.q: A study only includes 20-year-old students. What does this limit?

options.text: How far the results generalise to other groups (external validity)
options.feedback: Yes: results may not apply to older patients.
The study may still be well run internally.

topics.askClaude: Give me a short made-up abstract of an optometry study with a few deliberate weaknesses. Let me critique it with CASP-style questions, then reveal what I missed.

topics.title: Evidence-based practice
topics.summary: Evidence-based practice means combining the best available research with your clinical expertise and the patient's values and circumstances. Guidelines (NICE, College CMGs) do much of the evidence-gathering for you, but you still need to apply them thoughtfully.
keyPoints: Definition (after Sackett): integrating best research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values.
Five steps: Ask (a focused question), Acquire (search), Appraise, Apply, Assess (evaluate the outcome).
Frame questions with PICO.
Use pre-appraised sources first: guidelines, systematic reviews (e.g. Cochrane), College CMGs.
Patient values matter: the best treatment on paper may not suit a patient's life, budget or preferences.
Evidence changes — keep up to date through CPD.
Audit your own practice: are you doing what the evidence and guidelines say?
examTraps: Defining EBP as 'just following research'.
Ignoring patient preferences.
Relying on a single study when a systematic review exists.

diagram.description: Three overlapping circles: best research evidence, clinical expertise, patient values and preferences. The overlap in the middle is labelled evidence-based practice.

goDeeper.heading: A PICO example
goDeeper.body: P: children aged 6–12 with progressing myopia. I: myopia-control spectacle lenses. C: single vision spectacles. O: change in axial length over 2 years. Turning a vague question ('do these lenses work?') into PICO makes searching and appraising much easier.

goDeeper.heading: Guidelines in UK optometry
goDeeper.body: NICE guidelines (e.g. NG81 for glaucoma) and the College of Optometrists' Clinical Management Guidelines bring the evidence together for common conditions. Use them as your default, record when and why you depart from them, and check the date — guidelines are updated.

flashcards.back: Research evidence, clinical expertise, patient values.
Ask, Acquire, Appraise, Apply, Assess.
The Cochrane Library.
College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines.

mcq.q: Which is the best first source for a clinical question about managing blepharitis in UK practice?

options.text: The College of Optometrists' Clinical Management Guidelines

mcq.explanation: Start with high-quality pre-appraised sources (guidelines, systematic reviews) before individual studies.

mcq.q: Evidence-based practice combines which three things?

options.text: The best research evidence, clinical expertise, and the patient's values and circumstances

options.feedback: Patient values and expertise are central.
Research evidence is the first element.

mcq.q: In PICO, what does the C stand for?
Which source sits highest in the usual hierarchy of evidence for treatment questions?

options.text: A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs

options.feedback: Strong, but below a systematic review of several.

mcq.q: Write a PICO question: in myopic children, do atropine drops compared with placebo slow myopia progression? What is the 'O'?
Why aren't guidelines simply followed without thought?

options.text: They need applying to the individual patient's needs and preferences
options.feedback: Yes: that's the patient part of EBP.
Optometrists use College and NICE guidance.

mcq.q: A patient asks about a supplement with only one small, uncontrolled study behind it. What's the evidence-based response?

options.text: Explain the evidence is weak and discuss what's known honestly
Recommend it because there's some evidence

options.feedback: Weak evidence isn't proof of no effect.

mcq.q: Which is a pre-appraised source for quick clinical answers?

options.text: College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines

mcq.q: What's the first step in evidence-based practice?

options.feedback: Yes, then search, appraise, apply and evaluate.
That's expertise, not the first step.

mcq.q: Why does a systematic review search several databases and the grey literature?

options.text: To reduce the chance of missing studies, including unpublished ones (publication bias)
Because one database is always wrong

topics.askClaude: Help me turn 3 clinical questions I might have in clinic into PICO format, then suggest where I'd search for the answers.

topics.title: Using the library and literature search
topics.summary: From the library workshop in week 4: plan a search by splitting your question into concepts, listing synonyms, combining them with OR and AND, then filtering and checking sources against the assignment rules. Find disease information and guidance in the right places, and reference with Cite Them Right.
keyPoints: Narrow the topic to one question and identify its main concepts.
Different authors use different words, so list synonyms for each concept (e.g. optometry student, student optometrist, optometry programme; wellbeing, well-being, mental health, stress).
Join synonyms with OR (widens) and concepts with AND (narrows).
In Web of Science use filters (language, date), read abstracts, find PDFs via Google Scholar or Library Search, download straight away and keep folders organised.
For the vision sciences assignment the source must be a primary paper (no reviews; Web of Science marks reviews with an icon), within the date limit and at least 4 pages long.
Disease information: BMJ Best Practice, NHS pages (use a site: search), e-books and ClinicalKey. In guidelines and regulations, use Ctrl+F for the key terms the question points to.
Reference in Harvard style using Cite Them Right Online; book one-to-one help through the LibGuide.
examTraps: Using a review for the vision sciences assignment.
Using AND between synonyms, which loses relevant papers.

diagram.description: Venn diagrams: 'myopia OR nearsightedness' (both circles shaded — wider), 'myopia AND children' (only the overlap shaded — narrower), 'myopia NOT adults' (one circle shaded minus the overlap).

goDeeper.heading: E-portfolio weightings
goDeeper.body: The e-portfolio is 15% of OP2521: PHE task 4.5%, AaD 3%, DoC/PaP 3%, PPD 4.5%, plus pass/fail attendance at the primary care clinic and the IPL and communication skills sessions.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: other databases and tricks
goDeeper.body: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus and the Cochrane Library are other databases. Truncation (myop* finds myopia and myopic), phrase searching ("contact lens") and subject headings (MeSH) all help. Record your search strategy.

flashcards.back: OR widens (synonyms); AND narrows (combines concepts).
myop* → myopia, myopic, myopes.
MeSH (Medical Subject Headings).
So it's reproducible and can be reported in your methods.

flashcards.front: Rules for the vision sciences assignment source
flashcards.back: A primary paper (no reviews), within the date limit and at least 4 pages long.

mcq.q: Which search finds the MOST results?

options.feedback: An exact phrase is very narrow.

mcq.explanation: OR combines synonyms or related terms and returns anything with either.

mcq.q: You want papers on wellbeing in student optometrists. How do you combine 'wellbeing', 'well-being' and 'mental health'?

options.feedback: Yes: synonyms are joined with OR to widen the search.
AND narrows to papers containing all three.
Combining with OR is more efficient.

mcq.q: How do you combine the concepts 'optometry student' and 'wellbeing'?

options.feedback: Yes: AND finds papers that cover both concepts.
That would find papers about either.

mcq.q: Which source can't you use for the vision sciences assignment?

options.feedback: Yes: it must be a primary paper.

options.text: An experimental study of 14 patients with V1 damage
A paper published within the date limit
options.feedback: That's allowed if it's primary and long enough.

options.text: A study at least 4 pages long

mcq.q: Where would you look first for a reliable definition of bilateral diabetic retinopathy?

options.text: BMJ Best Practice or NHS pages
options.feedback: Yes: the library session's suggestions for disease information.

mcq.q: The assignment asks when the GOC must be informed about a health condition. What's the fastest way to find it in the guidance?

options.text: Open the relevant GOC document and search with Ctrl+F for the key terms
Read every GOC document from start to finish

mcq.q: Which referencing style and tool does the library recommend?

options.text: Harvard, using Cite Them Right Online
Any style, as long as it's consistent
options.feedback: The library points to Harvard via Cite Them Right.

mcq.q: You can't find a PDF for a paper found in Web of Science. What does the library suggest?

options.text: Paste the title into Google Scholar or Library Search
Use the abstract as your source
Pick a different paper at random

mcq.q: Why list synonyms for each concept?

options.text: Different authors use different terms, so you'd miss papers otherwise
Because databases need at least three words

options.feedback: You still use AND between concepts.

mcq.q: How much of the OP2521 module is the e-portfolio worth?

options.feedback: Yes: tasks A to D plus pass/fail attendance elements.
That's the PHE or PPD task alone.
That's the AaD or DoC/PaP task.

topics.askClaude: Help me build a PubMed search string for a question I'm working on: ask me the question, break it into concepts and synonyms, then build the Boolean string.

topics.title: The retina, LGN and visual pathways
topics.summary: How light becomes a neural signal and gets to the cortex. The retina is wired back to front, trades sensitivity against resolution through convergence, and sends its output mainly through the LGN to V1.
keyPoints: Visible light spans about 380 to 760 nm. Wavelength goes with hue, amplitude with brightness, purity with saturation. Light itself is not coloured.
Receptors hyperpolarise to light with graded potentials. Retinal ganglion cells are the first cells to fire action potentials.
About 120 million rods and 8 million cones per retina, but only about 1 million optic nerve fibres: average convergence 100:1.
Convergence is low in the fovea (good resolution) and high in the periphery (good sensitivity): a duplex system.
P-cells (about 80%): small, slow, small receptive fields, wavelength-sensitive. M-cells (about 10%): large, fast, large fields, flicker-sensitive, high contrast sensitivity.
Primary pathway: retina, chiasm, tract, LGN, optic radiation, layer 4C of V1. It carries about 90% of retinal output and each hemifield goes to the opposite hemisphere.
LGN: 6 layers. Top 4 parvocellular, bottom 2 magnocellular, koniocellular cells between. Only about 10% of its input is retinal.
examTraps: Saying the central fovea has all three cone classes. It has no blue cones (and no rods).
Treating the upside-down map in V1 as a problem the brain has to correct. It isn't one.
Calling the LGN just a relay. Most of its input is feedback from cortex and elsewhere, so it probably regulates the signal.

goDeeper.heading: Purkinje shift
goDeeper.body: Rods are most sensitive near 500 nm (blue-green) and cones near 550 nm (yellow). In daylight yellow flowers look lighter than green leaves; as night falls and rods take over, the leaves start to look lighter.

goDeeper.heading: The blind spot and filling in
goDeeper.body: The optic disc, 12 to 18° from the fovea, has no receptors. Each eye's blind spot is on the nasal retina so the two don't overlap, but even with one eye closed you see no hole because the visual system fills in from the surround. Something similar happens for blue in the central fovea: a tiny pure blue spot seen from far away looks black.

goDeeper.heading: Afterimages and size constancy
goDeeper.body: An afterimage has a fixed size on the retina, yet it looks larger when you look at a far wall than at a near sheet of paper. The visual system scales perceived size by perceived distance.

goDeeper.heading: Names for primary visual cortex
goDeeper.body: V1, striate cortex (for the visible stripe of myelinated axons), Brodmann's area 17, and calcarine cortex in clinical writing (much of it lies in the calcarine sulcus). The fovea is represented at the occipital pole.

flashcards.back: About 100 receptors to 1 ganglion cell. Lower in the fovea, higher in the periphery.

flashcards.front: Which retinal cells fire action potentials?
flashcards.back: Retinal ganglion cells. Receptors and most interneurons use graded potentials.
Six: top four parvocellular, bottom two magnocellular, koniocellular cells in between. Each layer takes input from one eye.
To the superior colliculus (midbrain) and to the pulvinar (thalamus).
The region of retina which, when stimulated, changes a cell's response (up or down).

flashcards.front: Size of the fovea and its rod-free centre
flashcards.back: Fovea 1.5 mm (5.2°); rod-free region 0.5 mm (1.7°).

mcq.q: The hue of light corresponds to its

options.feedback: Yes. Hue varies along the visible spectrum with wavelength.
Saturation is the purity of the wavelength: how far the colour is from white.
Intensity goes with the wave's amplitude.
Brightness goes with amplitude, not hue.

mcq.explanation: Week 3 test-your-knowledge question. Slide 3: wavelength with hue, amplitude with intensity, purity with saturation.

mcq.q: The central fovea

options.text: contains receptors that are most functional in bright illumination
options.feedback: Yes. It holds cones, which work at photopic levels.

options.text: contains three different classes of cones
options.feedback: There are no blue cones in the central fovea.

options.text: projects to cells with the greatest level of convergence
options.feedback: Convergence is lowest in the fovea, as low as 1:1 for some cells.

options.text: is used primarily for night vision
options.feedback: Night vision relies on the rod-rich periphery.

mcq.explanation: Week 3 test-your-knowledge question. Answer worked out from the lecture and handout: the central fovea is rod-free, has no blue cones and has the least convergence.

mcq.q: A retinal afterimage looks larger on a distant surface than on a near one because

options.feedback: Yes. The retinal image is fixed, so perceived size is scaled by perceived distance.
Lightness constancy is about surface reflectance, not size.
The effect is not retinal; the afterimage's retinal size is fixed.

options.text: the size of the retinal image changes
options.feedback: It doesn't: an afterimage is stuck to the same patch of retina.
Vergence may signal distance, but the reason the size changes is size constancy.

mcq.explanation: Week 3 test-your-knowledge question. The lecture uses afterimages as evidence for size constancy.

options.feedback: Yes. About 90% of retinal output takes this route.
A lesser pathway goes to the pulvinar.
A lesser pathway goes to the superior colliculus in the midbrain.
Not part of the primary visual pathway.

mcq.q: Rods are most sensitive at about 500 nm and cones at about 550 nm. What is the shift in sensitivity at dusk called?

options.feedback: Yes: greens look relatively lighter than yellows as light fades.
That's about surfaces under changing light.
That's different lights looking the same colour.

mcq.q: Why don't we notice our blind spots with both eyes open?

options.text: Each is on the nasal retina, so the two blind spots don't overlap
options.feedback: Yes, and the brain fills in even with one eye.

options.text: There are rods on the optic disc
The blind spots are in the fovea

options.feedback: Yes, serving about 100 times as many receptors.
That's roughly the number of rods.
That's roughly the number of cones.

mcq.q: Which retinal cells are the first to produce action potentials?

options.feedback: Yes: receptors and most interneurons use graded potentials.

mcq.q: What happens to the LGN's input?

options.text: Only about 10% comes from the retina; about 60% is feedback from cortex
options.feedback: Yes: so the LGN probably regulates rather than just relays.

options.text: All of it comes from the retina
Half comes from the superior colliculus
It has no input from cortex

cases.scenario: A friend says that because the image on the retina and the map in V1 are upside down, the brain must flip it the right way up.
cases.question: How would you answer using this lecture?
cases.modelAnswer: The cortical 'image' is not a picture that anything looks at; it is a pattern of neural activity. What matters is that the mapping is orderly (retinotopic), not which way up it is. So the inversion presents no computational problem to solve.

topics.askClaude: Explain The retina, LGN and visual pathways to me step by step, then quiz me on it.

topics.title: Receptive fields and convolution
topics.summary: A receptive field is a weighting function. When an array of cells applies the same weighting function across the whole image (convolution), the output is a neural image that marks edges, discards uniform areas, and exists at several spatial scales.
keyPoints: Receptive field: the region of retina which, when stimulated, changes the cell's response (up or down).
On-centre cells have an excitatory centre and inhibitory surround; off-centre the reverse. There are roughly equal numbers of each, and fields grow with eccentricity.
Response = light on excitatory regions minus light on inhibitory regions. With uniform light these cancel, leaving the spontaneous rate.
Responses: spontaneous discharge, a transient (phasic) burst at onset, then a sustained (tonic, steady-state) level.
Convolution: at every position multiply the image by the weighting function and sum. Convolving is a form of filtering.
Edges show up as zero-crossings in the neural image; uniform areas are discarded, which is data compression.
Different information sits at different spatial scales, so the retina produces overlapping neural images at several scales.
examTraps: Saying a receptive field is a region of the brain. It is a region of the retina (or visual field).
Thinking a centre-surround cell responds to uniform light. It responds only to a change in luminance within its field.
Confusing the steady-state (sustained) response with spontaneous discharge, which is the rate with no stimulus.

goDeeper.heading: Why the Hermann grid shows blobs
goDeeper.body: An on-centre cell centred on an intersection has light falling on more of its inhibitory surround (four arms) than one centred on a bar (two arms), so it responds less and signals less lightness. The blobs disappear at the intersection you look straight at, where fields are small.

goDeeper.heading: Negative numbers in neurons
goDeeper.body: Convolution with a centre-surround kernel produces positive and negative values. Neurons can't fire negatively, so spontaneous discharge acts as zero, and the on- and off-centre systems carry the two halves: two complementary neural images.

flashcards.back: Slide a weighting function (kernel) across the image; at each position multiply and sum to give one output value. The result is the neural image.

flashcards.front: Where is an edge in the neural image?
flashcards.back: At the zero-crossing between above- and below-spontaneous responses.

flashcards.front: Three jobs ganglion cells do by convolution
flashcards.back: Analyse at several spatial scales, highlight edges, and remove redundancy (compress data).

flashcards.front: Effect of widening a Gaussian weighting function
flashcards.back: More blur: fine detail is filtered out.

mcq.q: A receptive field is

options.text: the region on the retina that, when appropriately stimulated, changes a cell's response
the region in the brain that responds to stimulation in part of the visual field
options.feedback: It belongs to one cell and is defined on the retina, not in the brain.
Ganglion cell fields are roughly circular; cortical ones are typically elongated (coming in week 5).

options.text: the region of the visual field lit by electrical stimulation of the brain
options.feedback: That describes phosphenes, not receptive fields.

options.text: a place where visual experiments are done in the open air

mcq.q: A common explanation of the illusory blobs in the Hermann grid is that

options.text: centre-surround cells are stimulated differently by the bar and cross elements of the grid
options.feedback: Yes. At an intersection more of the surround is lit than on a bar, so on-centre cells respond less there.

options.text: on-centre cells are more active at the light intersections than off-centre cells
options.feedback: On-centre cells are less active at intersections than on bars, which is why the intersections look darker.

options.text: off-centre cells are more active at the light intersections than on-centre cells
options.feedback: The explanation compares cells at intersections with cells on bars, not on- with off-centre cells.

options.text: the centres of ganglion cells are similarly stimulated by light regions in the grid
options.feedback: The centres are similarly lit; it is the surround that differs.

mcq.explanation: Week 4 test-your-knowledge question 3. Worked out from the lecture and handout because the answer highlighting was lost.

mcq.q: Which is FALSE about the LGN?

options.text: The arrangement of the optic chiasm means each LGN views the ipsilateral visual field
options.feedback: This is the false one. Each LGN receives the contralateral visual field.
True: parvo layers (red/green) and konio layers (blue/yellow).

options.text: It has three layers per eye
options.feedback: True: six layers, alternating eye of origin.

options.text: It contains koniocellular cells between the magno and parvo layers
It is part of the thalamus

mcq.explanation: Week 4 test-your-knowledge question 4 (draws on the week 3 handout).

mcq.q: The process of 'looking through' a filter at an image is known as

options.feedback: Multiplication is one step inside convolution, which also sums at every position.
Summing is one step inside convolution.

mcq.q: A light spot falls on the inhibitory surround of an on-centre cell. What happens?

options.text: Its firing falls below spontaneous discharge
options.feedback: Yes: light on an inhibitory region reduces the response.
That's light on the excitatory centre.

mcq.q: Uniform light fills an on-centre ganglion cell's whole receptive field. What is its response?

options.feedback: Only if the centre alone were lit.
Only if the surround were lit alone.

mcq.q: In a neural image of a light/dark edge, where is the edge marked?

options.text: At the zero-crossing between above- and below-spontaneous responses

options.feedback: The peak sits just beside the edge.

mcq.q: What happens to an image as the Gaussian weighting function gets wider?

options.feedback: Yes: fine detail is filtered out.

mcq.q: Which three jobs do ganglion cells do through convolution?

options.text: Analyse at several spatial scales, highlight edges and remove redundancy

options.feedback: Not the three jobs in the lecture.

options.text: Fire action potentials, transduce light and store images

cases.scenario: An array of on-centre ganglion cells views a vertical edge, light on the left and dark on the right.
cases.question: Describe the response of cells across the array and explain each part.
cases.modelAnswer: Far left (all light) and far right (all dark): spontaneous rate, because centre and surround cancel or neither is stimulated. A cell centred exactly on the edge: also spontaneous, as centre and surround get equal light. Just left of the edge: the centre is fully lit but part of the surround is dark, so less inhibition and a response above spontaneous. Just right of the edge: the centre is dark but part of the surround is lit, so the response falls below spontaneous. The edge is marked by the zero-crossing between these, and the uniform areas carry no extra signal.

topics.askClaude: Explain Receptive fields and convolution to me step by step, then quiz me on it.

topics.title: Primary visual cortex (V1)
topics.summary: V1 turns the retina's centre-surround code into orientation-selective responses, organised into modules that each analyse one small patch of the visual field for orientation, eye of origin and colour.
keyPoints: Retinotopic but distorted: about half of V1 represents the central 10° of the visual field.
V1 is the first stage with orientation selectivity. Most cortical cells have little or no background firing.
Simple cells: elongated, separate excitatory and inhibitory regions; selective for orientation, size and position (phase).
Complex cells: no separate on and off regions; orientation- and size-selective but respond anywhere in the field; non-linear; like moving or flickering stimuli.
End-stopping (once called 'hypercomplex') prefers contours that end in the field and occurs in simple and complex cells.
Orientation columns make up a hypercolumn covering all orientations at one location. Population responses, not single cells, code orientation; the tilt aftereffect is evidence.
Ocular dominance columns alternate between the eyes; cytochrome oxidase blobs at their centres hold colour-selective (double-opponent) cells. About 2,500 modules of about 100,000 cells.
examTraps: Calling simple cells 'edge detectors': they respond to bars of either polarity too, so their response is ambiguous.
Thinking one cell's firing tells you orientation. Contrast and orientation are confounded; you need the population.
Saying blob cells are sharply orientation-tuned. They are broadly tuned or untuned.

goDeeper.heading: How the maps were found
goDeeper.body: 2-deoxyglucose is taken up by active cells, so after showing an animal a stimulus, autoradiography of cortical slices reveals which cells responded: this gave the retinotopic map (Tootell et al., 1982). Injecting a tracer into one eye gives alternating stripes: ocular dominance columns (LeVay et al., 1975). Staining for cytochrome oxidase, a metabolic enzyme, reveals the blobs (Tootell et al., 1983). Optical imaging later confirmed and extended these maps.

goDeeper.heading: The tilt aftereffect as a population code
goDeeper.body: Stare at a tilted grating and the cells tuned to that tilt get tired. A vertical test pattern then excites a population whose peak is pushed away from the adapted orientation, so vertical looks tilted the other way. A system of single feature detectors would predict no such shift.

flashcards.back: Simple: separate on and off regions, sensitive to exact position. Complex: no separate regions, responds to the right orientation and size anywhere in its field.
A group of V1 orientation columns that together cover all orientations for roughly the same part of the visual field.

flashcards.front: How are ocular dominance columns revealed?
flashcards.back: Inject a radioactive tracer into one eye and autoradiograph V1: alternating labelled and unlabelled stripes.
Cytochrome-oxidase-rich patches in the centres of ocular dominance columns: colour-selective, low spatial frequency, poorly tuned for orientation.

mcq.q: Simple cells

options.text: respond to stimuli at specific retinal coordinates
options.feedback: Yes. Each has a receptive field at a fixed place on the retina.

options.text: respond to stimuli at specific head- or body-centred coordinates
options.feedback: Their fields are retinotopic, so they move with the eye.

options.text: respond to stimuli anywhere in the visual field
options.feedback: Each covers only a small patch.

options.text: respond only if the organism is gazing in a specific direction
options.feedback: Gaze direction doesn't gate their response.

mcq.explanation: Week 5 test-your-knowledge Q1 (answer worked out from the lecture).

mcq.q: Complex cells

options.text: respond best to stimuli of the right size and orientation placed anywhere within their receptive field
options.feedback: Yes: orientation- and size-selective but indifferent to position.

options.text: have receptive fields organised in opponent fashion, like simple cells
options.feedback: They lack distinct on and off regions.

options.text: respond best to a moving line of any orientation

options.feedback: They are a main class of V1 cell.

mcq.q: An orientation hypercolumn is

options.text: a group of V1 cells processing different contour orientations at similar positions in the visual field
a single column of cortical cells with the same orientation preference
options.feedback: That is one orientation column; a hypercolumn is a full set.

options.text: a column of neurons in the parietal lobe
options.feedback: It is in V1, in the occipital lobe.
It is an anatomical and physiological structure; psychophysics gives indirect evidence for population coding.

mcq.q: Hubel and Wiesel injected a radioactive amino acid into one eye and autoradiographed V1. They saw

options.text: alternating stripes of radioactivity and non-radioactivity

options.feedback: Each eye projects to both hemispheres.

options.text: bands called thick and thin stripes
options.feedback: Those are V2 cytochrome oxidase stripes.
The tracer is carried through the LGN to V1.

mcq.q: A simple cell's field is uniformly lit. Part of its inhibitory region is then made darker. What happens?

options.feedback: Yes. Less light on an inhibitory region means less inhibition.
That would follow from darkening the excitatory region.

options.text: It responds at its spontaneous level
options.feedback: That was the case before the change, with uniform light.
The balance between regions has changed.

mcq.explanation: Week 5 test-your-knowledge Q8, using the week 4 rule for summing excitatory and inhibitory regions.

mcq.q: Which is FALSE about the modular organisation of visual cortex?

options.text: Destroying the modules in V1 causes achromatopsia
options.feedback: False: losing V1 causes blindness in that part of the field, not selective loss of colour.

options.text: There are enough modules for a 50 × 50 patchwork
Each module has a pair of ocular dominance columns
Cells between blobs are selective for size and orientation

mcq.q: Which is FALSE about blob cells?

options.text: Most of them are narrowly tuned for orientation
options.feedback: False: orientation tuning in blobs is broad or absent.
True: that's how blobs are seen.

options.text: They are found in the centres of ocular dominance columns

mcq.q: If a cortical cell responds to a vertical luminance contour

options.text: some aspect of the stimulus is being represented in the visual system
options.feedback: Yes. That's all a single response tells us.

options.text: the organism will see a vertical contour
options.feedback: One cell's response doesn't guarantee perception, and it is ambiguous on its own.

options.text: the cell must be a simple cell
options.feedback: Complex cells respond to contours too.

options.text: the cell must have a centre-surround receptive field
options.feedback: Most V1 cells have elongated, orientation-selective fields.

mcq.q: How much of V1 represents the central 10° of the visual field?

options.feedback: Yes: the map is stretched in favour of the centre.

mcq.q: Why can't a single simple cell's response code orientation?

options.text: Contrast and orientation are confounded: a medium response could mean several things
Simple cells don't respond to orientation
Simple cells only fire to colour

topics.askClaude: Explain Primary visual cortex (V1) to me step by step, then quiz me on it.

topics.title: Beyond V1: the ventral ('what') stream
topics.summary: After V1, vision splits into specialised areas and two broad streams. The ventral stream (V1 to V2 to V4 to IT) builds up the representation of form, colour and objects, and damage to it causes specific agnosias.
keyPoints: Over 30 visual areas with over 300 connections. Moving up, receptive fields grow, maps get cruder and selectivity becomes more complex; there is feedback throughout.
Two streams (Ungerleider and Mishkin): ventral 'what' to the temporal lobe (IT), dorsal 'where' to the parietal lobe (e.g. area 7a).
Evidence: retrograde tracers in parietal and temporal cortex label almost separate cells earlier on (Baizer et al., 1991); parietal damage gives Balint's syndrome, temporal damage gives agnosia.
V2: cytochrome oxidase thick stripes (stereo), thin stripes (colour) and interstripes (form). Many V2 cells respond to illusory contours; V1 cells don't.
V4: crude map, colour columns (globs), some colour constancy, and cells tuned to curves. Damage causes achromatopsia.
IT: 'elaborate' cells for combinations of features, and face-selective cells; a face is probably coded by about 100 cells together.
examTraps: Calling face cells 'grandmother cells'. Each responds to many faces; identity is in the population.
Taking prosopagnosia as proof of a face area without a fair within-class comparison (e.g. a farmer recognising individual cows).
Saying all V4 cells are colour blind, or that V4 does only colour.

goDeeper.heading: Seven clinical conditions
goDeeper.body: Cortical blindness (V1 damage), blindsight (responding to things not consciously seen), optic ataxia (trouble reaching), ocular apraxia (trouble directing the eyes), simultanagnosia (seeing only one object at a time); the last three together make Balint's syndrome. Visual agnosia (failing to recognise objects) and prosopagnosia (faces) come from temporal damage; achromatopsia (colour loss with form preserved) from V4 damage.

goDeeper.heading: Illusory contours in V2
goDeeper.body: Peterhans and von der Heydt drifted Kanizsa-type figures across V2 receptive fields. Cells fired to real edges and to illusory edges, but not when the 'pac-men' gaps were closed or only half the figure was shown. Because the response tracks the perception, the contour may be built bottom-up in V2 rather than only inferred by higher areas.

flashcards.back: Optic ataxia, ocular apraxia and simultanagnosia, after parietal (dorsal stream) damage.
Thin stripes: colour (from V1 blobs). Thick stripes: stereo. Interstripes: form (from V1 interblobs).
Complete loss of colour vision with form preserved: V4 damage.
IT cells that respond to particular combinations of complex spatial features (Tanaka, 1993).

mcq.q: Being unable to recognise the faces of your own family is called

options.feedback: That's the parietal triad of optic ataxia, ocular apraxia and simultanagnosia.

mcq.q: Responding to objects in the visual field that you say you can't see is called

options.feedback: Yes: seen after V1 damage, probably via routes that bypass V1.
In agnosia the object is seen but not recognised.
A parietal disorder of reaching, gaze and attention.

mcq.q: Moving up the cortical hierarchy, which is FALSE about visual neurons in general?

options.text: You can predict their responses to complex stimuli from their responses to small spots of light
options.feedback: False: higher cells are non-linear and need complex stimuli to characterise.

options.text: Their retinotopic maps become less precise
Their stimulus selectivities become harder to characterise

mcq.q: Which is FALSE?

options.text: All cells in V4 are colour blind
options.feedback: False: V4 has colour columns and its damage causes achromatopsia.

options.text: Parts of V1 a few mm apart encode different retinal regions
Parts of IT a few mm apart encode different kinds of image feature
options.feedback: True: IT has columns for different features.

options.text: Neighbouring V1 columns prefer different orientations

mcq.q: Which is TRUE?

options.text: Many cells in V2 respond to illusory contours
End-stopped cells only respond to contours that extend beyond their receptive field
options.feedback: The reverse: they prefer contours that end inside the field.

options.text: Simple cells respond to any visual stimulus
Primate retinal ganglion cells are direction-selective

options.feedback: M-cells are not wavelength-selective; P-cells are.

mcq.q: Elaborate cells respond to

options.feedback: Yes: IT cells described by Tanaka.

options.text: oriented contours anywhere in their receptive field
options.feedback: That describes complex cells in V1.

options.text: complex motion such as expansion and rotation
options.feedback: That's MST, in the dorsal stream.

options.text: faces, tuned to the head's gaze angle
options.feedback: Face cells are a different IT population.

mcq.q: Where do V2 thin stripes get their main input?
Damage to V4 is linked with which condition?

options.feedback: Yes: complete colour loss with form preserved.

mcq.q: Why is prosopagnosia not straightforward proof of a dedicated face area?

options.text: Faces need within-class discrimination, so a fair test needs other within-class tasks (e.g. a farmer's cows)

mcq.q: Retrograde tracers injected into parietal and temporal cortex (Baizer et al., 1991) showed what?

options.text: Almost no earlier cells contained both tracers, so the two streams are largely separate
The tracers only reached the LGN

topics.askClaude: Explain Beyond V1: the ventral ('what') stream to me step by step, then quiz me on it.

topics.title: Beyond V1: the dorsal ('where'/'action') stream
topics.summary: The parietal route from V1 through MT and MST to area 7a analyses motion and space, and may be better thought of as guiding action than locating objects.
keyPoints: MT (V5): receptive fields of 5–10°, columns for direction of motion, sensitivity to relative motion, depth from motion and disparity.
V1 codes the separate components of a plaid; MT 'pattern cells' code the overall motion we actually perceive.
Akinetopsia (motion blindness) follows damage to MT on both sides.
MST: fields of 30–50°, tuned to expansion, contraction, rotation and spirals, as in optic flow during self-motion.
Coordinate frames: retinocentric, egocentric and allocentric. 7a has gaze-locked cells; PO has 'real position' cells whose fields aren't fixed on the retina.
Zeki: four pathways (motion, colour, form with colour, form without colour), with cross-talk; V3 doesn't fit what/where.
Milner and Goodale: ventral = perception, dorsal = action. DF (ventral damage) could post a card through a slot but couldn't report its orientation; optic ataxia (dorsal damage) is the reverse.
examTraps: Saying the dorsal stream simply handles moving objects and the ventral stream stationary ones.
Giving DF's damage as dorsal: it was ventral (visual form agnosia).
Treating blindsight as evidence that V1 is where seeing happens: it shows V1 is needed for awareness, not that awareness happens there.

goDeeper.heading: Population coding capacity
goDeeper.body: Four cells, each with five distinguishable response levels, can in principle signal 5 × 5 × 5 × 5 = 625 different combinations. That is why about 100 face cells could code a very large number of faces.

goDeeper.heading: Perception versus action in healthy people
goDeeper.body: Aglioti et al. (1995) reported that grip aperture wasn't fooled by the Titchener (Ebbinghaus) size illusion even though perception was, which fits the action/perception split. Franz et al. (2000) couldn't replicate it, and Haffenden and Goodale (2000) disputed their stimuli. The question is still open.

flashcards.back: Motion blindness: seeing the world as a series of snapshots. Needs damage to MT on both sides.
The pattern of motion on the retina as we move (expansion moving forward, rotation turning the head); MST cells are tuned to these patterns.
Egocentric: position relative to yourself. Allocentric: position relative to other objects or the room.
M cells, then V1 layer 4B (and V2 thick stripes), then MT.

options.text: V1 is also known as area 17

options.feedback: Area 18 is V2; striate cortex is V1.

options.text: V6 is also known as MT
options.feedback: MT is V5; V6 is PO.

options.text: IT is also known as V7

mcq.q: Which is true?

options.text: Part of V5 is thought to be specialised for motion
Part of IT is specialised for knowing where objects are
Part of MST is specialised for colour
Part of V4 is specialised for faces

mcq.q: Real position cells

options.text: have receptive fields that move about the retina
options.feedback: Yes: they code a position in space, so the retinal location changes with gaze.

options.text: respond to stimuli at specific retinal coordinates
respond only if the animal looks in a specific direction
respond to stimuli outside the visual field

options.feedback: Yes, as do thick stripes and V1 blobs.

options.text: Regions receiving input mainly from one eye
options.feedback: Ocular dominance columns are shown by tracers, not CO.

Which is true of the two-pathway model?

options.feedback: Yes: the action stream guides behaviour quickly.

options.text: The ventral stream handles motion perception
The ventral stream directs visually guided actions
options.feedback: That's dorsal in Milner and Goodale's view.

options.text: The ventral stream deals with stationary objects and the dorsal with moving ones
options.feedback: Too simple: the split is about what the output is for.

mcq.q: Patient DF (Milner and Goodale): where was the damage and what happened?

options.text: Ventral stream; DF couldn't judge orientation perceptually but acted as if she could
options.feedback: Yes: she posted a card through the slot but couldn't report its angle.

options.text: Ventral stream; DF could judge orientation but couldn't act on it
Parietal stream; DF could judge orientation but couldn't act on it
options.feedback: That describes optic ataxia, not DF.

options.text: Parietal stream; DF couldn't judge orientation but acted as if she could

options.feedback: That assumes one face per cell, a grandmother-cell code.

mcq.q: What is akinetopsia?

options.text: Motion blindness, after damage to MT on both sides

mcq.q: Which area's cells prefer expansion, rotation and spiral motion?

options.feedback: Yes: useful for optic flow when moving through the world.

topics.askClaude: Explain Beyond V1: the dorsal ('where'/'action') stream to me step by step, then quiz me on it.

topics.title: Perceptual grouping and visual search
topics.summary: Mid-level vision links local features into surfaces and objects. The Gestalt rules describe how elements group, figure-ground segregation separates objects from backgrounds, and visual search experiments show which features the brain codes in parallel.
keyPoints: Gestalt rules: proximity, similarity, good continuation, closure, symmetry, common fate (elements moving together group).
Prägnanz ('good figure'): we see the simplest structure possible, but simplicity is hard to define or compute.
Rules compete with no fixed order: proximity can beat similarity or lose to it.
Figure-ground: border-ownership cells in V2 help decide which side of an edge is the object.
Contour linking: smooth chains of aligned elements are easy to see, which suggests an 'association field' in V1/V2.
Feature search is parallel (pop-out; reaction time flat as distractors increase); conjunction search is serial (reaction time rises).
Enns and Rensink (1990): search can be parallel for 3D orientation, so grouping uses depth and Marr's strictly feed-forward stages can't be right.
examTraps: Saying the Gestalt rules explain grouping: they describe it.
Assuming pop-out only reflects V1 features.

goDeeper.heading: Running a visual search experiment
goDeeper.body: Measure reaction time to find a target among different numbers of distractors. A flat line means parallel search (the target pops out); a line rising with each extra distractor means serial search, item by item.

flashcards.back: Elements that move together are grouped together.
The 'law of good figure': every pattern is seen as the simplest structure possible.
Finding a target defined by two features (e.g. green and horizontal) among distractors sharing one; reaction time rises with the number of distractors.
2D image features, then surfaces, then 3D objects, in a strictly feed-forward sequence.

mcq.q: A shape only becomes visible when it moves relative to its background. This is grouping by

options.feedback: That's about shared features such as colour.

mcq.q: Border ownership

options.feedback: Yes: it signals which side of an edge belongs to the figure.

options.text: is another name for grouping by proximity
is a natural consequence of texture segmentation

mcq.q: In a search where the target is a conjunction of two features and each distractor has one of them, you'd expect

options.text: the task to take longer as the number of distractors increases
reaction time to stay the same whatever the number of distractors
conjunction detectors in V1 to draw attention to the target

mcq.q: Dots arranged in pairs close together are seen as pairs. Which rule is this?

options.feedback: That's grouping by shared features such as colour.

mcq.q: A curving line is seen as one continuous path where it crosses another line. Which rule?
What does Prägnanz state?

options.text: We see the simplest structure the pattern allows

mcq.q: What does Rubin's vase demonstrate?

options.text: Figure-ground segregation can flip between two interpretations

mcq.q: In a feature search (one horizontal line among verticals), what happens to reaction time as distractors increase?

options.text: It stays roughly flat (pop-out, parallel search)

mcq.q: Field, Hayes and Hess (1993) found what about contours?

options.text: Chains of aligned elements are easy to see, but equally regular non-aligned chains are hard
options.feedback: Yes: vision has a built-in code for smooth contours.
They're mathematically equal but perceptually not.

mcq.q: What problem did Enns and Rensink's (1990) results cause for Marr's model?

options.text: Search was nearly parallel for 3D orientation, so grouping uses depth, not just 2D features
options.feedback: Yes: Marr's strictly feed-forward stages can't be right.

topics.askClaude: Explain Perceptual grouping and visual search to me step by step, then quiz me on it.

topics.title: Lightness perception
topics.summary: We perceive the lightness of surfaces (reflectance), not the amount of light reaching the eye. The visual system recovers reflectance from luminance ratios at edges, anchoring, and its interpretation of shadows and 3D layout.
keyPoints: L = I × r (luminance = illuminance × reflectance). The retina receives only L.
Lightness refers to surfaces; brightness refers to light. Lightness constancy: surfaces look the same under different illumination.
The ratio of neighbouring luminances equals the ratio of their reflectances, whatever the illumination.
Anchoring: assume the lightest region is white to turn relative values into absolute lightness.
Ganglion cells respond strongly to sharp luminance changes and weakly to gradual ones, which explains the Craik-O'Brien-Cornsweet illusion and lightness contrast.
Fuzzy shadow edges (penumbras) aren't treated as reflectance changes; perceived 3D layout can change perceived lightness (Adelson) and the reverse (crater/volcano).
examTraps: Calling lightness a physical quantity: it's psychological. Luminance, illuminance and reflectance are physical.
Writing L = r ÷ I instead of L = I × r.

flashcards.back: I × r: luminance = illuminance × reflectance.
Lightness: perceived reflectance of a surface. Brightness: perceived intensity of light.
Assuming the lightest region in view is white, so other greys can be scaled from it.

mcq.q: With L = luminance, r = reflectance and I = illuminance, which is correct?
Which is NOT a physical property of the world?

options.feedback: Yes: it's the perception of reflectance.

mcq.q: Which IS a physical property of the world?

options.text: Whether something looks near or far
Whether something is on the left or right

mcq.q: A white surface (100% reflectance) and a dark one (10%) are seen first in bright light and then in dim light. What stays the same?

options.feedback: Yes: that's why ratios can recover relative reflectance.
The difference shrinks in dim light.

mcq.q: What does 'anchoring' mean in lightness perception?

options.text: Assuming the lightest region in view is white
options.feedback: Yes: it turns relative values into absolute lightness.

mcq.q: Why does the Craik-O'Brien-Cornsweet illusion work?

options.text: Ganglion cells respond to sharp luminance changes but hardly to gentle gradients
options.feedback: Yes: the cusp edge produces a response like a real step.

options.text: The two regions really differ in luminance
options.feedback: They're the same apart from the edge.

mcq.q: Why aren't shadow edges usually seen as changes in surface reflectance?

options.text: Their fuzzy penumbra tells the visual system it's a shadow
options.feedback: Yes: blacking out the penumbra makes it look like a stain.

options.text: Shadows are only seen in colour

mcq.q: Adelson's checker-shadow illusion shows that

options.feedback: Yes: the 'shadowed' square looks lighter though it's the same grey.

options.text: ganglion cells explain all lightness effects
shadows always make things look darker
options.feedback: Here they make a square look lighter.

mcq.q: The crater/volcano picture shows what about lightness and layout?

options.text: Perceived shading can determine perceived 3D shape
options.feedback: Yes: the reverse of Adelson's effect.

options.text: Both are processed only in V1
